title: Order slips under the door
allegory: Tool use is like someone in a sealed room who can only pass notes under the door: a menu card says what can be ordered and how to write the slip, a helper outside runs each order and slides the answer back, and the card is all they ever see of the kitchen.
map: someone in a sealed room who can only pass notes
the model: it can only emit text, never run anything itself
the menu card pinned inside the door
the tool schema: name, argument types and docstring, built by Inspect's @tool
an order slip written in the menu's format
a tool call: the tool's name plus its arguments
the helper who runs it and slides the answer back
your code: execute() runs, and the result returns as a tool message
a menu that never says what a failed order looks like
a Returns line without the failure shape: the model retries the same failing call

chapters.name: All words, no hands
chapters.note: can explain the sum, can't press the buttons

cap.1: A model can explain long multiplication beautifully and still get a big sum wrong. It only produces words. It can't pick up a calculator.
cap.2: An LLM's only output is text. Tool use turns some of that text into a structured request your code runs, so the model can get exact results and act.
cap.3: Function calling is the single mechanism that turns text output into a side effect. Every agent loop in [3.4] and control protocol in [3.5] sits on top of it.

cap.1: Picture someone in a sealed room with a menu card on the door. They write an order slip, slide it out, and a helper runs it and slides the answer back.
cap.2: You pass tool definitions alongside the messages. The model replies with a tool call; your code runs it and returns the result as a tool message. Then it carries on.
cap.3: Five steps: pick the function, describe it as a schema, pass the definitions as tools, read the tool call out of the response and execute it, feed the result back.

cap.1: Round and round: the model asks, your code does it, the answer comes back, and the model decides whether to ask again or simply reply.
cap.2: If the response contains tool calls, execute each, append the results as tool messages and generate again. If it contains none, that is the final answer.
cap.3: The ReAct variant adds a lever: tool_choice='none' for the reasoning turn, so the model thinks without acting, then a normal generate for the action turn.

cap.1: The model never sees your code. It sees a card: the tool's name, what each input should look like, and what comes back. That card is all it has.
cap.2: Inspect builds the schema from the function name, type hints and docstring, Args block and Returns line included. That schema is what enters the model's context.
cap.3: Models are fine-tuned to read tool descriptions the way they read system and user messages, so the docstring is a prompt, not documentation.

chapters.name: Vague card, precise card

right.title: Written as all it gets
lines: one line on what it does
Returns: '8', or what an error looks like

chapters.verdict: If you can't tell from the schema alone how to call it, neither can the model.

cap.1: A vague card gets vague slips, like 'add those numbers up please'. Say exactly what to write, with an example, and the orders come right first time.
cap.2: With no Args block the model guesses the format from the parameter name. With no failure shape in Returns it can't tell an empty result from an error.
cap.3: Then agents retry the identical failing call until the message limit trips. In the WikiGame, MovePageTool must say its title comes from get_permitted_links's exact output.

chapters.name: Blame the card first
chapters.note: model 'can't do it'? read the card first

cap.1: When an agent flops, check the menu card before blaming the diner. A test of the model can quietly turn into a test of your instructions.
cap.2: The classic symptom: the model never calls your tool, or sends arguments your executor can't parse, and you conclude it doesn't understand the task.
cap.3: Tools, like elicitation, are scaffold levers: a vague schema turns a capability measurement into a measurement of your own string handling.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Check the scaffold before the model

cap.1: Tools are how models act in the world: search, run code, click. Knowing what they read, and where it breaks, is part of steering what they do.
cap.2: Toolformer (Schick et al., Meta AI, 2023) showed a model could learn when to call a calculator, search engines, a translator or a calendar from a few demonstrations per API.
cap.3: It improved zero-shot performance, often competitive with much larger models, without losing core language ability: tool access is a capability multiplier separate from scale.

coda.title: Match each part of a tool to its job
pairs: wraps your function so Inspect can build its schema
the instructions the model actually reads
each input's exact format, with an example like '3+5'
what success looks like, and what failure looks like
the result handed back so the model can carry on
a turn to think without acting

caption.1: Pair each part of a tool with its job. The cards are shuffled every play, so it's the meaning that has to stick, not the position.
caption.2: Every pair is a piece of the loop: signature and docstring become the schema, the model's tool call comes out, and the result goes back as a tool message.
caption.3: The schema is prompt text: the name, per-argument descriptions from Args, and the Returns description. tool_choice decides whether a turn may call tools at all.

where_else: Agent scaffolds, where every step of the loop is a tool call and a tool message
AI control protocols, which monitor and edit the same tool calls before they run
Capability evals, where a vague tool schema can make a capable model look weak

hamming.what: Tool use is handing a model described functions it can ask you to run, then running them and returning the results, so it can act rather than only talk.
hamming.when: Whenever a task needs exact computation, fresh information or side effects: calculators, search, code execution, and every agent loop.
hamming.why: It is the single mechanism that turns text into action, so it multiplies capability and also defines exactly where an agent can reach.

object.title: The order loop
object.subtitle: Messages and menu cards go in, order slips come out, answers come back, until the model simply replies.

cap.1: The whole loop. Messages and menu cards go into the model; order slips come out; answers come back in.
cap.2: Tool definitions travel with the messages. The model's output is either a tool call or a final answer.
cap.3: One generate call per turn; tool results are appended as tool messages before the next.

cap.1: The menu cards, up close. They're built from your docstrings, and they're all the model knows about your tools.
cap.2: Inspect's @tool reads the signature, type hints and docstring and turns them into the schema the model sees.
cap.3: Name, per-argument descriptions from Args, and the Returns description: prompt text, not documentation.

cap.1: Follow one order: the model writes 3+5, your code works it out, 8 comes back as a new message, and the model carries on.
cap.2: Parse the tool call, run execute() with its arguments, append the result as a tool message, generate again.
cap.3: The model folds the returned result into its next tokens, as Toolformer learned to do self-supervised.

cap.1: No slip this time: the model answers directly, and the loop ends.
cap.2: A response with no tool calls is the final answer; your loop stops generating.
cap.3: tool_choice='none' guarantees a turn with no tool call; in the ReAct variant that turn is for reasoning, not the final answer.

predict.q: The model never calls your new tool. First thing to check?

options.t: Print the schema and read it cold

predict.why: The schema is all the model sees. If you can't tell how to call the tool from it, neither can the model.

predict.q: Your tool errors, and the model repeats the identical call until the message limit. Likely cause?

options.t: The Returns line never says what failure looks like

predict.why: It can't tell an error from an empty result, so it tries again.

predict.q: What does the model actually see of your tool?

options.t: Its name, argument types and docstring, as a schema

predict.why: Inspect builds the schema from the signature, type hints and docstring; your code never enters the context.

object.where: Any system that acts through a described interface: the label on the door is the only instruction that gets read.
